title: What I Learned from My Students This Semester
author: Jonathan Boymal
summary: Jonathan Boymal marks a batch of university reflections on a Google antitrust case study and finds that the most valuable learning happened where the theory met the lives students had lived outside class. Many discovered they had never chosen their search engine, and finance students began to doubt that a durable moat signals good management. He connects this to Dewey, Moll's funds of knowledge, Vygotsky and Immordino-Yang's work on reflection and the brain's default mode network. The strongest reflections ended with open questions, which he reads as a sign of learning that tolerates uncertainty, a stance AI-supplied instant answers make harder. Drawing on Mezirow, Bridges, Rosa's idea of resonance and Buber, he argues that reflective assignments invite students into an honest relation with their own experience and the educator into the role of witness. He closes by naming what education is for: protecting the interval between impulse and action in which a person can say, wait, let me think.
points: Students who reflected on their own habits found that the availability of a choice had been mistaken for the exercise of one, which is the case study's central lesson made personal.
Learning grew where lived experience from family, work and culture met the discipline's theory, echoing Dewey, Moll's funds of knowledge and Vygotsky.
Open-ended reflections that end in questions signal deep engagement, and tolerating uncertainty is harder when AI supplies instant answers.
Resonance, in Rosa's sense, cannot be engineered or scheduled, but it tends to appear when learners are open, attention has room, and friction is present.
Education should protect the pause between impulse and action, and reflective assignments make the educator a witness to a student in the process of becoming.
quotes: Many of them have been trained to produce the correct answer efficiently, and reflection asks for something slower.
This is the central illusion of the digital economy. We take the availability of a choice for the exercise of one.
In my students’ writing, learning happened where the theory on the page met the life they had lived outside the classroom.
Uncertainty is uncomfortable. It also sharpens focus, strengthens memory and prepares the mind to revise its view, and the gap between a question and an answer gives thought room to develop.
Each of those endings is a way of saying I don’t know, and that has become harder to say. The Greek philosopher Socrates treated it as the foundation of wisdom.
Resonance cannot be engineered, though it does not arrive at random. It tends to appear when learners are open, when there is room for attention, and when the encounter feels meaningful.
My rubric had no criterion for what I had been handed, and my authority as a marker sat awkwardly beside the writer’s candour.

Rereading these reflections reminded me what I think education is for. It can build the conditions under which changes in belief become possible and it can make room for the interval between impulse and action, in which a person can look at the algorithmic feed, the default search engine and the frictionless output, and say: Wait. Let me think.
